speaker: Scott Kirby
title: Scott Kirby - United Airlines CEO
question: In commercial aviation, why do flight delays so easily snowball into widespread cancellations across an airline's network?
guest: At United, it's worked well because we built a system to repair crews. That's what happens at an airline. If you get weather delays or any kind of delays, you have an impact to irregular operations—IROPS is what we call it. If you have IROPS, it can snowball on you because of crews being out of place, and there's all kinds of legal rules about how many hours they can work and all kinds of things that can foul that up. You've got an airplane that has—sometimes a widebody airplane has three pilots and might have ten flight attendants—and if one of them doesn't make it, the whole flight gets canceled. So that's the really complex thing. We've built really good automation to keep that from happening in an event like this. Some other airlines struggled with it over the weekend, but our crews mostly stayed in pretty good shape and healthy.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Delays snowball because airlines schedule their aircraft, crews, and airport slots as tightly interlocked chains with very little slack.

A single plane typically flies four to six legs a day, so a late morning departure pushes back every later flight that aircraft was due to operate. Crews are a separate chain: pilots and flight attendants often switch aircraft during the day, so one late inbound flight can strand the crew needed for a different plane. Crews also face legal duty-time limits; once delays push them past those limits, they "time out" and cannot fly, and replacement crews may not be in the right city.

Hub-and-spoke networks amplify this. Disruption at one hub (weather, air traffic control restrictions, a technical outage) hits hundreds of connecting flights at once, and gates fill with planes that cannot leave, blocking arrivals.

At that point, aircraft and crews are out of position across the network. Airlines then cancel flights deliberately to reset the schedule, because trying to run everything late would carry the disruption into the next day. High load factors mean few spare seats, planes, or reserve crews to absorb the shock.

Modern airlines run tightly coupled networks designed to maximize asset utilization, leaving very little slack when disruptions hit. Individual aircraft typically fly several legs a day with minimal turnaround buffers, so a single delayed arrival immediately pushes back subsequent departures across multiple cities. Because pilots, flight attendants, and planes often follow separate itineraries rather than staying together all day, one late inbound flight can stall multiple outbound flights waiting on either an aircraft or a crew member.

Rolling delays turn into outright cancellations largely because of strict regulatory crew duty-time limits. Once cumulative delays push pilots or flight attendants past their maximum legal working hours, they "time out" and cannot fly until they complete mandatory rest. With few spare aircraft and reserve crews—mostly stationed only at major hubs—disrupted flights elsewhere often have no replacements, leaving planes and staff out of position for later schedules. Compounded by gate shortages, air traffic caps, and nighttime airport curfews, airlines frequently cancel flights preemptively to halt the cascade, reposition displaced crews and aircraft, and reset the network.

Flight delays snowball because airline networks are tightly linked and run with very little slack. One aircraft usually flies several legs a day, so a two-hour delay on the morning flight carries into every later leg, which is called delay propagation. Crews are tied together in a similar way, and they often switch planes during the day. A late inbound flight can strand a pilot or flight attendant who was supposed to work a different outbound flight, which spreads the disruption to aircraft that had no problem of their own.

Federal duty-time limits make it worse. Once delays push crews past their legal hours, they "time out" and can't fly. Reserve crews are limited and are often in the wrong city. Hub-and-spoke scheduling packs flights into tight connection banks, so trouble at one hub affects the whole system. Planes and crews also end up out of position for the next day.

Airlines often cancel flights on purpose to stop the spread and reset the operation. Scheduling software that can't keep up with mass disruptions can turn that into a meltdown, as with Southwest in December 2022.

At that point, canceling some flights lets the airline free up resources and get aircraft and crews into position for the next day. Otherwise, the same disruption can carry into the morning schedule.

quotes: If an inbound flight is late, the aircraft may miss its next departure, and its crew may miss a separate assignment.

points.why: The response identifies legal duty limits as a constraint that can make delayed crews ineligible to operate subsequent flights.
